items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>generation</radical> radical and the <kanji>generation</kanji> kanji are the same, and since the people of one generation are the people of one world, it also means world or society.
items.reading_mnemonic: Whatever Sei has to <reading>say</reading> comes out as a smug little 「<reading>せい</reading>」, and today's is that her <kanji>generation</kanji> is smarter than every one that came before it.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>rice field</radical> so tightly <radical>jammed in</radical> by fences on every side becomes its own private <kanji>world</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A surveyor named <reading>Kai</reading> barks 「<reading>かい</reading>」 each time her tape measure claims another field, and she will not rest until the whole <kanji>world</kanji> is fenced into tidy squares.

items.mnemonic_text: A roof gathering people below it: a meeting, to meet.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> who walks the trail head-down and a <radical>cloud</radical> parked at face height are bound to <kanji>meet</kanji> with a soft, damp bump.
items.reading_mnemonic: Up where the trail vanishes into low cloud, a hiker named <reading>Kai</reading> has set up beside the one vending machine. Every climber who finally reaches him calls out <reading>かい</reading>, so his name is also the sound two people make when they meet.
items.description: 会 and 今 share the same wide, person-shaped lid on top. Under the lid, 会, meet, carries a full boxy shape with a bar across it and more strokes stacked below. 今, now, has almost nothing under the lid, just one short hooked stroke like a tiny 7 and no bar.

items.mnemonic_text: A box repeating the same shape inside: the same.
items.meaning_mnemonic: When every <radical>mouth</radical> shut inside a <radical>wide box</radical> eats off one flat <radical>ground</radical>, no bowl can be bigger than another, so all their meals come out the <kanji>same</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A lazy baker called <reading>Dough</reading> refuses to swap his single cutter, grunting 「<reading>どう</reading>」 as he claims every bun is the <kanji>same</kanji> as the last.

items.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>idea</kanji> is a stray <radical>sound</radical> that gets stuck playing on a loop inside your <radical>heart</radical> until you finally do something about it.
items.reading_mnemonic: A tiny inventor called <reading>Eee</reading> can't hold in a single <kanji>idea</kanji> without letting out the squeal 「<reading>い</reading>」 that gave her the name, so the whole lab knows the second she's had one.

items.mnemonic_text: A hand holding a skewer of tasks: a matter to handle.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>matter</kanji> is whatever an animal's <radical>snout</radical> has pinned to the <radical>ground</radical> and its <radical>mouth</radical> has sunk a <radical>barb</radical> into, so it can never be dropped.
items.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank a fisherman hooks something huge, and each time the line jerks he grunts <reading>じ</reading>, which is just <reading>gee</reading> with the air knocked out of him. Whatever it is has swallowed the barb and will not shake loose, so it is his problem now, dragging him through the mud.
items.description: The 'thing' here is always an intangible one: a matter, an affair, an event, something that happens or that you have to deal with. A physical object you can pick up is a different word entirely. With its kun'yomi it is the ordinary spoken word for an abstract 'thing'.

items.mnemonic_text: A nose pointing at oneself: 'me', self.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You get this one for free, because the <radical>self</radical> radical you already know and the <kanji>self</kanji> kanji are the exact same character.
items.reading_mnemonic: A genie drifts up from the offering box at Grandma Kane's shrine, and when you ask who he takes orders from, he points a finger straight at his own nose and says <reading>じ</reading>. It comes out like a flat <reading>Gee</reading>, the sound you make when the answer was always going to be yourself.
items.description: All three are a tall box with inner lines. 自 has a short slanted stroke on top and two inner lines, splitting it into three parts. 目, eye, has those same three parts but no stroke on top. 白, white, has the top stroke but only one inner line, so it splits into two.

items.mnemonic_text: An altar (示) marking earth (土): a shrine, and by extension a company.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Give a <radical>cult</radical> its own fenced patch of <radical>earth</radical> and it turns respectable overnight, whether you call the result a <kanji>company or shrine</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A door-greeter named <reading>Sha</reading> can't tell a <kanji>company or shrine</kanji> apart, so she bows and chirps 「<reading>しゃ</reading>」 at every gate on the street and hopes one of them hires her.

items.mnemonic_text: Legs launching outward from a bow: departure, emitting.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Off the blocks, the <radical>outspread legs</radical> explode sideways. The racer's <radical>human legs</radical> land planted wide just as <radical>two</radical> chopsticks clatter off a dropped bento — chasing a train already <kanji>departed</kanji>, hissing steam as it pulls away without them.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the platform, a conductor named <reading>Hatsu</reading> slams the doors and yells <reading>はつ</reading> into his whistle as steam bursts from the wheels — one word, and the train is already gone.

items.mnemonic_text: An old man bent over a stick: a person.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Any heap of used-up <radical>day</radical>s tall enough to stand up and grumble about turning <radical>old</radical> is what we call a <kanji>person</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The konbini greeter <reading>Shah</reading> barks 「<reading>しゃ</reading>」 at every <kanji>person</kanji> who crosses the mat, because counting each one past the beeping till is the only job management ever gave him.
items.description: Almost always a suffix meaning 'one who does something' — a worker, a scholar, a young person. Standing alone it is a blunt, formal word for a person, closer to 'individual' than to an everyday 'someone'.

items.mnemonic_text: Earth (土) twisting like a snake (also): the ground.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>ground</kanji> is just <radical>earth</radical> with a <radical>snake tail</radical>'s knack for staying exactly where it is while everything else moves on.
items.reading_mnemonic: A clumsy cheetah on the mountain trail face-plants so much that her teeth squeak 「<reading>ち</reading>」, the <reading>chee</reading> in cheese, every time her chin meets the <kanji>ground</kanji>.
items.description: This is earth as in the ground underfoot, the soil, or a region of land — not the planet Earth, which needs a second kanji for 'globe' added after it.

items.mnemonic_text: A workbench stacked with tools: one's trade, business.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Turning the stiff <radical>bristles</radical> you comb off a <radical>sheep</radical> into hairbrushes nailed to a <radical>tree</radical>-stump counter is a strange little <kanji>business</kanji> that somehow pays.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi liked those sheep-bristle hairbrushes so much he now sells them right by the onigiri shelf, his first real side business. The barcode scanner he calls <reading>Gyo</reading> screeches <reading>ぎょう</reading> each time a brush slides past the beeping till.

items.mnemonic_text: A flag on a pole pointing a direction.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>direction</radical> radical and the <kanji>direction</kanji> kanji are the same, and it also works as a polite word for a person, since pointing someone's way is a soft way to point them out.
items.reading_mnemonic: Where the shrine path splits three ways, an old gardener leans on his <reading>hoe</reading> and never says a word. Ask him which fork to take and he simply swings the hoe to point down one of them with a low, breathy <reading>ほう</reading>.
items.description: The look-alike is 万, ten thousand. 万 has one flat top line, only three strokes, and a last stroke that sweeps far out to the lower left. 方 adds a short cap stroke above the top line and a crossbar through the middle, and its hooked last stroke stays short and tucked in.

items.mnemonic_text: Earth (土) where the sun (陽 implied) opens up a place.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>sunbeam</radical> breaks through and lands on one square of bare <radical>earth</radical>, and that lit-up patch is now a <kanji>place</kanji> you can point to.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every morning a hiker called <reading>Joe</reading> climbs to the lone vending machine and plants himself on the exact patch of dirt the sun reaches first. He grunts <reading>じょう</reading> at anyone who edges toward it. That scrap of lit ground is the only spot on the mountain he will call a real place.

items.mnemonic_text: An axe (斤) beside a door (戸): the place where work is done.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Any patch of dirt becomes a <kanji>place</kanji> the moment you hang a <radical>door</radical> on it and bury an <radical>axe</radical> in the stump beside that door so the spot is pinned for good.
items.reading_mnemonic: Realtor <reading>Shaw</reading> will sell you any <kanji>place</kanji> at all, since his entire sales pitch is one long, confident 「<reading>しょ</reading>」 and he lets the buyer picture the rest.

items.mnemonic_text: A stylized heart shape with three drips of feeling.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>heart</radical> radical and the <kanji>heart</kanji> kanji are one and the same, and because old Japanese placed thought in the chest rather than the head, the shape also means mind.
items.reading_mnemonic: Shin the jogger stops at Grandma Kane's shrine every morning to complain about his <reading>しん</reading>, his aching <reading>shin</reading>. One morning a cat on the mossy steps trips him, and the fall finally gives his hammering heart something else to worry about.
items.description: The one to watch is 必 (necessary). Both have the same curved, swooping base and a scatter of short dots, but 必 drives a straight diagonal stroke right through the center of the shape, running down toward the lower left. 心 has nothing crossing it: just the open curved base and three separate dots resting around it. If a line spears through the middle, you are looking at 必, not 心.

items.mnemonic_text: A roof (广) over a stopping point (占): a shop.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The moment you charge people for <radical>fortune-telling</radical> under your flimsy roadside <radical>shelter</radical>, it has become a <kanji>shop</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A shopkeeper called <reading>Ten</reading> won't let you out of her roadside <kanji>shop</kanji> until you have bought exactly 「<reading>てん</reading>」 things, counting each one on her fingers.

items.mnemonic_text: A roof over a pig (豕): the traditional house.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Any <radical>roof</radical> with a <radical>pig</radical> sprawled on its back under it is a <kanji>house</kanji>, since you only bring livestock indoors where you live.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Kaa</reading>, the fire-breathing crow, croaks 「<reading>か</reading>」 from the power line and a stray puff of flame floats down onto the nearest <kanji>house</kanji>, which is why the whole street keeps its buckets full.
items.description: Beyond the building, 家 also means the household living in it, and as a suffix it marks an expert or professional rather than a house at all.

items.mnemonic_text: A roof (宀) reaching (至) to enclose a room.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>room</kanji> is the patch of floor under a <radical>roof</radical> where your journey finally <radical>arrive</radical>s and you drop your bags.
items.reading_mnemonic: A hotel maid called <reading>Sheets</reading> has been handed every <kanji>room</kanji> on the floor and mutters 「<reading>しつ</reading>」 as she unlocks each new door.
items.description: 室 is the formal 'room' in names for purpose-built rooms, not the everyday word for a room at home.

items.mnemonic_text: A box enclosing plotted lines: a diagram, a map.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You cannot <radical>mow</radical> a walled <radical>enclosure</radical> into a tidy striped pattern without a <radical>small</radical> <kanji>diagram</kanji> of it in your hand.
items.reading_mnemonic: A zookeeper named <reading>Zoo</reading> is so hopeless among the identical pens that she keeps the whole park's <kanji>diagram</kanji> inked on her arm and jabs it, going 「<reading>ず</reading>」, at every fork in the path.

items.mnemonic_text: Words (言) given a式 (form/ceremony): a formal test.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A formal <radical>style</radical> of <radical>speech</radical>, one hard question after another, is how you put a student to the <kanji>test</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Shizu</reading> the taste-tester sucks air through her teeth with a sharp 「<reading>し</reading>」 every time the chef puts another over-salted broth to the <kanji>test</kanji> on her tongue.

items.mnemonic_text: A horse (馬) inspected all over (侴): to test, examine.
items.meaning_mnemonic: To <kanji>examine</kanji> a <radical>horse</radical> properly, you need a whole <radical>assembly</radical> of vets, because one person can never check every hoof and tooth at the same time.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Ken</reading> the sword-collecting shiba barks a flat 「<reading>けん</reading>」 at every blade you bring him, since he will not let one onto his wall until he has <kanji>examine</kanji>d it for rust.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>construction</radical> radical and the <kanji>craft</kanji> kanji are the same, and since raising a building takes the same skilled hands as any other craft, one character does for both.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi insists his no-wasted-motion restocking is a real <kanji>craft</kanji>, so he does it in a carpenter's <reading>coat</reading> and barks a proud 「<reading>こう</reading>」 as each shelf snaps into place.

items.mnemonic_text: An old man's staff (攵) guiding a child (孝): to teach.
items.meaning_mnemonic: To <kanji>teach</kanji> is to drill <radical>filial piety</radical> into a child with one bamboo <radical>tap</radical> until propping the old man upright feels natural.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the school, the cane-happy teacher everyone calls <reading>Kyo</reading> opens each lesson by making you haul a sandbag 'grandpa' across the field. Every time he barks your name, you chant <reading>きょう</reading> straight back at him.

items.mnemonic_text: A field (田) sitting over the heart (心): thoughts forming.
items.meaning_mnemonic: To <kanji>think</kanji> is to let your <radical>heart</radical> plow the same square <radical>rice field</radical> of a worry back and forth until something finally grows.
items.reading_mnemonic: A librarian called <reading>Shi</reading> hisses 「<reading>し</reading>」 at anyone who dares to <kanji>think</kanji> out loud, because in her reading room every thought stays locked behind your teeth.

items.mnemonic_text: A bow (弓) with its string pulled taut: to pull.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Hooking a straight <radical>stick</radical> behind a <radical>bow</radical>'s string and hauling back until the whole bow bends double is exactly what it means to <kanji>pull</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the school sports field, the archery captain <reading>Lynn</reading> leans her full weight back against a bow no one else can bend. As she drags the string to her cheek she lets out a strained <reading>いん</reading>, and the team knows that sound means the pull is near breaking point.

items.mnemonic_text: Repeated breaths (可可) beside a yawning mouth (欠): a song.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>song</kanji> is what you get when your <radical>big brother</radical> starts a <radical>yawn</radical> so wide that it turns into a tune halfway through.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow lands on the power line above the school field to join the children's singing. Every time she opens her beak, the note comes out as a burnt <reading>か</reading>. It is a <reading>caw</reading> with a puff of flame that scorches the grass below.

items.mnemonic_text: A hand (扌) keeping something steady like a temple (寺): to hold.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>hand</radical> that can <kanji>hold</kanji> an entire <radical>Buddhist temple</radical> down on its measured plot of ground has a grip that never slips.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the temple, the old monk makes you hold the huge bronze bell over your head while he counts the yard stones. Soon your arms shake so hard that the only sound you manage is <reading>じ</reading>. It is the flat <reading>gee</reading> anyone groans under a weight they cannot put down.
items.description: In its continuous form it also means to have or own, so possessing a car or a pet counts as hold too.

items.mnemonic_text: A person (亻) directing an official (吏): to use, to employ.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>use</kanji> a <radical>person</radical> the moment you make them your <radical>officer</radical> and start sending them out to do the errands you would rather skip.
items.reading_mnemonic: A mynah bird called <reading>Shishi</reading> copies every order it overhears, so you <kanji>use</kanji> it to wake the whole house at dawn while it screeches 「<reading>し</reading>」 between shouts.

items.mnemonic_text: A person (亻) in motion (動): working.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The one <radical>person</radical> still on the <radical>move</radical> after the whole group has flopped down in the shade is the only one actually doing <kanji>work</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, she settles in among the cats while the one helper she calls <reading>Dough</reading> sweeps every mossy step, polishes the giant bell, and refills all the lanterns by himself. Each heave on the bell-hammer drags a tired <reading>どう</reading> out of him.
items.description: This is one of a small set of kanji coined in Japan, not borrowed from China. It adds the person radical to the 'move' character, the idea being that a person in motion is a person at work.

items.mnemonic_text: A person (亻) relying on old (昔) favors: to borrow.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> walking off with what they need today and putting off paying it back until it feels like <radical>once upon a time</radical> is how you <kanji>borrow</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, borrows a rickety <reading>shack</reading> from the person down the road and never gives it back. Every time the owner comes asking, Kaa just croaks <reading>しゃく</reading> from the power line and singes the eviction notice to ash.
items.description: 借 covers renting as much as borrowing — money, an apartment, a bike, anything you take now and promise to give back or pay for. English splits borrow and rent; this kanji does both.

items.mnemonic_text: Money (貝) replacing (代) what's missing: to lend.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>lend</kanji> by handing your <radical>money</radical> to a <radical>substitute</radical> owner who stands in your place and must return every coin.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, guards a pile of coins on the power line above Koichi's konbini and only lends to people who look smart. You knot a proper <reading>tie</reading> at your neck, so he leans down, croaks <reading>たい</reading>, singes the knot to mark it, and drops the loan in your hands.

items.mnemonic_text: An arrow (矢) hitting the mouth's (口) point: to know for certain.
items.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's sports field, an <radical>arrow</radical> streaks across the grass and thunks dead center into the target. In that same instant, your <radical>mouth</radical> snaps open with the answer, just the fact flying out as fast and true as the shot. That instant, certain hit is <kanji>knowing</kanji> something.
items.reading_mnemonic: Chibi the parrot roosts on that same target and shrieks <reading>ち</reading> the second the arrow lands, confirming the answer before you can even say it out loud — a sharp <reading>chee</reading> of certainty every time.

items.mnemonic_text: A woman (女) with her own (台) fresh start: to begin.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Nothing can <kanji>begin</kanji> until the <radical>woman</radical> running the ceremony climbs onto the <radical>pedestal</radical>, because the crowd only quiets down once it can see who is in charge.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Shino</reading> the race starter lost her pistol, so now she just shouts 「<reading>し</reading>」 to <kanji>begin</kanji> each race, and half the runners are still tying their shoes when it starts.

items.mnemonic_text: Thread (糸) wound to its winter (冬) finish: to end.
items.meaning_mnemonic: When the reel's last bit of <radical>thread</radical> runs out just as <radical>winter</radical> arrives, both the sweater and the year reach their <kanji>end</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The theatre usher <reading>Shoo</reading> waves both arms and barks 「<reading>しゅう</reading>」 to force the <kanji>end</kanji> of every late-night film, hurrying the last viewer up the aisle.

items.mnemonic_text: Grasping (⺈) at the heart (心): an urgent hurry.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>hurry</kanji> when a pounding <radical>heart</radical> drives you into a low <radical>crouch</radical> with your <radical>snout</radical> already aimed at the door.
items.reading_mnemonic: A stagehand named <reading>Cue</reading> screams 「<reading>きゅう</reading>」 the instant the curtain lifts, so the whole cast has to <kanji>hurry</kanji> because his cue always lands a beat too late.

items.mnemonic_text: A person (土-like legs) bounding forward: to run.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You break into a <kanji>run</kanji> because the <radical>earth</radical> baking under your shoes will not let you <radical>stop</radical> moving for even one second.
items.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, the midday sun turns the dirt to a griddle. A hiker named <reading>Sew</reading> feels it burn through her boots, cannot stand still for even a breath, and sprints for the vending machine at the top, yelping <reading>そう</reading> with every stride.

items.mnemonic_text: Wings spread mid-motion: to fly.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>fly</radical> radical and the <kanji>fly</kanji> kanji are the same character, a point you earn just by knowing your radicals.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Hina</reading> the hang-glider pilot shoves off from the top of the mountain trail, sure she will soar this time. She clips the lone vending machine on the way past and drifts down going <reading>ひ</reading>, a long thin wheeze, before the bushes catch her.

items.mnemonic_text: Water (氵) poured over first (先) rinse: to wash.
items.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Before</radical> any meal you hold your hands under running <radical>water</radical> for a moment, and that first quick rinse is the <kanji>wash</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank a laundry-worker called <reading>Sen</reading> scrubs shirts against a flat rock all morning. Each time one comes clean she flings it onto the line and barks <reading>せん</reading> for the next. By noon the rope sags with washed shirts and her throat is raw from shouting it.

items.mnemonic_text: Bad luck (歹) beside a person collapsed: to die.
items.meaning_mnemonic: When your <radical>bad luck</radical> runs deep enough to bend the <radical>spoon</radical> before it reaches your lips, the next thing you do is <kanji>die</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Nurse <reading>Shh</reading> shushes every patient the second they start to <kanji>die</kanji>, hissing 「<reading>し</reading>」 so the rest of the ward never hears the bad news.

items.mnemonic_text: A wandering road (辶) with a flag (斿) of fun: to play.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Drifting like a <radical>swim</radical>mer down whatever <radical>road</radical> opens next, with no place you have to be, is exactly <kanji>play</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: After the last bell a kid called <reading>Yu</reading> never walks straight home. His friends stand out on the sports field yelling <reading>ゆう</reading> until he drifts over to whichever game is loudest. One game bleeds into the next, and that is his whole afternoon, every afternoon.

items.mnemonic_text: Sheep (羊) settling onto the eye's (目) view: to arrive, to wear.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Cut one <radical>slash</radical> down a whole <radical>sheep</radical>, pull the fleece around you until it hides an <radical>eye</radical>, and you <kanji>wear</kanji> the animal itself.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kiki, the tree spirit, giggles inside her old oak while you wrestle into the fresh sheep-fleece coat. She pokes a branch out and gives the hem one hard <reading>chuck</reading> downward to seat it on your shoulders, laughing <reading>ちゃく</reading> as the collar flops over your eyes.
items.description: One character, two senses that feel unrelated: to put on or wear clothing, and to arrive at or reach a place. The wear sense uses the kun reading; the arrive sense shows up in travel words for arrival and landing. It is normal to be thrown that the same character means both.

items.mnemonic_text: A road (辶) that splits away (韋): to differ.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Every strip of <radical>tanned leather</radical> you <radical>advance</radical> past on the riverbank path is dyed a shade off from the last, so all of them <kanji>differ</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At that same riverbank, a dyer named <reading>Evie</reading> pulls the drying strips down two at a time and holds them up to the sun. The moment a pair does not match, she snaps out a sharp <reading>い</reading> and dunks one straight back in the river.
items.description: In everyday speech, the verb form of this kanji often means simply 'no, that's wrong,' not a neutral 'these differ.' Used to answer someone, it corrects them and can sound blunt.

items.mnemonic_text: A bird (隹) landing on a tree (木) with the flock: to gather.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Every <radical>old bird</radical> too stiff to fly still manages to hop over and <kanji>gather</kanji> on the one <radical>tree</radical> whose branches hang low enough to reach.
items.reading_mnemonic: The school photographer yells 「<reading>しゅう</reading>」, the way other people blurt <reading>shoot</reading>, to <kanji>gather</kanji> every squirming kid onto the bleachers for the group photo.

items.mnemonic_text: A knife (刂) cutting a shape (另) apart: to separate.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A single stroke of the <radical>knife</radical> cuts the <radical>wrap</radical> holding the bundle shut, and each hungry <radical>mouth</radical> ends up with a <kanji>separate</kanji> share.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the school bake sale a girl called <reading>Betsy</reading> will not pass a tray along until she has sliced it. She saws each slab into portions, muttering <reading>べつ</reading>, almost her own name, at every cut, so no two buyers get the same piece. The wrap ends in a heap and each share leaves on its own plate.
items.description: The gloss is 'separate', but 別 just as often means 'another' or 'different', as in a different day or a separate room. Used as a verb with its kun'yomi it means parting from a person: seeing someone off, or breaking up with them.

items.mnemonic_text: A lamp's flame steady atop its stand: the main, central one.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Screw a <radical>lid</radical> down over the <radical>king</radical>'s crown and you seal in the one <kanji>lord</kanji> whose word the whole house has to follow.
items.reading_mnemonic: A footman called <reading>Shoe</reading> greets just one man each morning with a crisp 「<reading>しゅ</reading>」, since that is the only <kanji>lord</kanji> whose boots he is paid to kneel over.
items.description: Under its top dot, this is exactly 王 'king / jewel': three bars crossed by a standing post. 王 has nothing above its top bar; 主 adds one short dot there. Lose that dot and you have written king, not lord.

items.mnemonic_text: A mouth (口) atop legs (儿): the elder brother who speaks first.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>older brother</kanji> is just a big <radical>mouth</radical> propped up on two <radical>human legs</radical>, always tall enough to talk over you first.
items.reading_mnemonic: A bossy boy called <reading>Kay</reading> drills the younger kids until they greet him as 「<reading>けい</reading>」, because the <kanji>older brother</kanji> is the one who decides what everyone else is allowed to call him.

items.mnemonic_text: A cord wound down a post: the younger, lower-ranked brother.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>younger brother</kanji> is kid number <radical>eight</radical>, so all he inherits is a thin <radical>slash</radical> of cake and a round of tired <radical>condolences</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A caterer called <reading>Tay</reading> only ever shouts 「<reading>てい</reading>」 when he hands the smallest plate to the <kanji>younger brother</kanji>, since the runt of the family always eats last.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>gate</radical> radical and the <kanji>gate</kanji> kanji are the same, and because heavy cannons once stood guard in fortress gateways, the very same character is used to count them.
items.reading_mnemonic: The rabbit twins Mon and Bun wedge themselves in the shrine <kanji>gate</kanji> and refuse to pass through until their book argument is settled, each <reading>moan</reading>ing a stubborn 「<reading>もん</reading>」.

items.mnemonic_text: A woman (女) who is already (市-like) senior: the older sister.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>older sister</kanji> is the one <radical>woman</radical> in the house old enough to be sent to the <radical>market</radical> alone with the grocery money.
items.reading_mnemonic: Being oldest, the <kanji>older sister</kanji> gets left in charge, so she keeps the little ones quiet with one sharp 「<reading>し</reading>」. It is the same <reading>shh</reading> a librarian would use, and the only word they hear all evening.
items.description: Both put the woman 女 on the left, so the right side is the only tell. Here it is the market 市: a flat top stroke over a small box with one vertical dropping straight through. In the look-alike 妹 'younger sister' the right side is a tree shape instead, with two crossbars and diagonal legs that splay out wide.

items.mnemonic_text: A woman (女) not yet (未) grown: the younger sister.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>woman</radical> who is <radical>not yet</radical> old enough for anyone to call her one is the <kanji>younger sister</kanji> of the house.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine a toddler chases every cat down the mossy steps, grabbing fur and howling <reading>my</reading>, my, mine, which comes out of her as <reading>まい</reading>. She is too little to know the shrine cats belong to no one. Grandma Kane scoops her up before she reaches the big bell.
items.description: The look-alike is 姉, 'older sister'. Both share the 'woman' element on the left, so the difference is all on the right. 妹 has 'not yet': a tree with two crossbars, the upper shorter, and two short diagonals flaring out at the foot like roots. 姉 instead has a small tick atop a boxy cloth shape, with one long vertical dropping straight through and out the bottom, and no flaring feet.

items.mnemonic_text: Standing (立) by a tree (木) watching (見): a parent's love.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At the edge of Sei's school field, someone has climbed a <radical>tree</radical> and wedged themselves to <radical>stand</radical> on the highest branch. They crane forward to <radical>see</radical> every second of the match without missing a kick. That straining figure, who won't leave until it's over, is a <kanji>parent</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: When the final whistle blows, they scramble down too fast and bark their <reading>しん</reading> — their <reading>shin</reading> — hard against a branch, then limp off still cheering about the goal.

items.mnemonic_text: A person kneeling beside a seal: the color of one's mood.
items.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Color</kanji> is what you get when you <radical>crouch</radical> over a puddle and <radical>swirl</radical> every leftover paint pot into it at once.
items.reading_mnemonic: An electrician named <reading>Shock</reading> grabs a bare wire, yelps 「<reading>しょく</reading>」, and sees every <kanji>color</kanji> he never knew existed flash across the inside of his eyelids.

items.mnemonic_text: A mouth (口) not yet (未) full: tasting a bit.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A bite sitting in your <radical>mouth</radical>, chewed but <radical>not yet</radical> gone down, still holds every bit of its <kanji>taste</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini a food blogger tries the free onigiri sample and holds the bite on her tongue, humming <reading>み</reading> as if singing <reading>me</reading>, me, only me. She refuses to swallow until she has named every flavour, so the taste just goes on and on while the till beeps.
items.description: Beyond literal taste, 味 carries the figurative flavour of a thing. It sits inside the common words for 'meaning' and for 'interest', where it points at what something is really like rather than how it tastes on the tongue.

items.mnemonic_text: A woman (女) beside her child (子): a fondness, to like.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>woman</radical> who will put down anything to pick her <radical>child</radical> back up is the dictionary picture of <kanji>fond</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Koichi</reading> is so <kanji>fond</kanji> of a tidy onigiri shelf that he lets out a soft 「<reading>こう</reading>」 every time he squares one up, which is as close as he gets to admitting he loves anything.

items.mnemonic_text: A twisted shape over the heart (心): a bad feeling.
items.meaning_mnemonic: When something the size of <radical>Asia</radical> is parked on top of one small <radical>heart</radical>, the only word for how that feels is <kanji>bad</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi's night clerk <reading>Aku</reading> grunts 「<reading>あく</reading>」 at every carton he shelves, and by morning each one he touched has gone <kanji>bad</kanji>.
items.description: In casual speech this word doubles as a quick 'my bad' apology, not a claim that something is evil. The first time someone says it right at you, they are saying sorry.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>mask</radical> radical and the <kanji>mask</kanji> kanji are the same, and since a mask is only a face you can take off, the character also means the face or features behind it.
items.reading_mnemonic: Menzo the actor wears a <kanji>mask</kanji> for every role so that behind it he could be any of a hundred <reading>men</reading>, and he crows 「<reading>めん</reading>」 at anyone who claims to know which.

items.mnemonic_text: Big (大) with an extra drop of size: thick, fat.
items.meaning_mnemonic: One extra <radical>drop</radical> of fat on someone already stretched as <radical>big</radical> as they can stand is all it takes to turn big into <kanji>fat</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The one necktie in Sei's school lost-and-found has been knotted so many times its knot swelled <kanji>fat</kanji>, and 「<reading>たい</reading>」 is the only name anyone gives that sad <reading>tie</reading> now.
items.description: 太 is 大 'big' with a single dot added low, tucked into the fork between the legs. Plain 大 has no dot at all. In 犬 'dog' the dot sits high, up at the top-right corner, not down in the fork.

items.mnemonic_text: Thread (糸) drawn out fine over a field (田): thin, detailed.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Every mud path splitting a <radical>rice field</radical> into squares is laid no wider than a single strand of <radical>thread</radical>, so each divider comes out impossibly <kanji>thin</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The tailor <reading>Sigh</reading> splits one hair down its length just to prove his stitches are still <kanji>thin</kanji> enough, then lets out a long, smug 「<reading>さい</reading>」.

items.mnemonic_text: A cart (車) that passes lightly (圣): not heavy.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>holy</radical> hand laid flat on a loaded <radical>vehicle</radical> draws the weight out like a blessing, until the <kanji>light (weight)</kanji> cart drifts a finger off the road.
items.reading_mnemonic: A kid named <reading>Kay</reading> runs after the blessed cart as it drifts down the road a finger off the ground. Every time it bobs higher she shouts <reading>けい</reading>, which is her own name and the exact sound Japanese gives the letter K.

items.mnemonic_text: A cart's heavy load stacked high: heavy, important.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>village</radical> told to shift a <radical>thousand</radical> rice sacks finds out fast that a thousand of anything at once is too <kanji>heavy</kanji> to move.
items.reading_mnemonic: The village hires a furniture mover named <reading>Jude</reading> to bring its thousand rice sacks up from the riverbank in one load. He gets three sacks onto his back, sinks to his knees in the mud, and stays there groaning <reading>じゅう</reading> until the tide comes in.
items.description: The one to watch is 車 (car / vehicle). 車 is symmetrical: one upright stroke runs straight down through a single boxed grid, with a short bar above and below. 重 breaks that balance. Its top has a slanted lid stroke, and an extra horizontal bar cuts across the full width partway down. The widest line sits at the very bottom, so the whole character looks low and bottom-heavy.

items.mnemonic_text: Two bent bows losing their tension: weak.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Draw the string on a <radical>bow</radical> carved from <radical>ice</radical> and it snaps in your hand, because a frozen weapon is a <kanji>weak</kanji> one.
items.reading_mnemonic: The cheap folding car <reading>jack</reading> from the vending machine at the top of the mountain trail sinks straight back down under the first wheel. The driver mutters 「<reading>じゃく</reading>」 at a lift too <kanji>weak</kanji> to do its one job.
items.description: Tacked onto the end of a number, this kanji flips from 'weak' to 'a little under'. A count with it on the tail means just below that figure, not a feeble version of it.

items.mnemonic_text: A bow (弓) reinforced with a hard shell (虽): strong.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Thread that an <radical>insect</radical> spun inside its <radical>cocoon</radical> is tougher than steel wire, so a <radical>bow</radical> strung with it comes out impossibly <kanji>strong</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kyo, a retired weightlifter, hauls the shrine's giant bell rope once and lifts the whole frame off its posts. Grandma Kane sighs that no word but 「<reading>きょう</reading>」, short for <reading>Kyo</reading>, is <kanji>strong</kanji> enough for the man.
items.description: After a quantity, this kanji reads 'and a bit more' rather than 'strong'. An amount with it on the end sits just over the round number, not far above it.

items.mnemonic_text: The sun (日) hidden behind sound (音) of night: dark.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A room with its <radical>sun</radical> switched off, where you steer only by <radical>sound</radical>, is the very definition of <kanji>dark</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Ann, the mole, shuffles across the pitch-black room feeling along the wall until she finds the switch marked <reading>on</reading>. She flicks it again and again and nothing happens, so she groans <reading>あん</reading> and goes back to steering by sound in the total dark.

items.mnemonic_text: The sun (日) beside the moon (月): both lighting up, bright.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The sky stays <kanji>bright</kanji> when the <radical>sun</radical> will not go home and the <radical>moon</radical> shows up early, so both lights are on at once.
items.reading_mnemonic: A lighthouse keeper called <reading>May</reading> chirps 「<reading>めい</reading>」 the instant she throws the switch, certain the beam will never blaze <kanji>bright</kanji> unless her voice cues it first.

items.mnemonic_text: A shelter (广) opening onto open ground: wide, spacious.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A cliffside <radical>shelter</radical> holding nothing but one silkworm's <radical>cocoon</radical> is almost all empty air, so the bare floor stretches out absurdly <kanji>wide</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi the konbini king rips out half his shelving and lets out a triumphant <reading>koh</reading>, 「<reading>こう</reading>」, because only a <kanji>wide</kanji> aisle lets him push two restock carts through side by side.

items.mnemonic_text: Water (氵) breaking through a levee (夬): a decisive break.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Once the <radical>water</radical> droplet leaves the brush and the hooked arm that means <radical>decide</radical> starts to swing, both are past pulling back, which is what it is to <kanji>decide</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A diner cook called <reading>Ketch</reading> freezes with the ketchup bottle tipped and barks 「<reading>けつ</reading>」 until you <kanji>decide</kanji>, because his committed pour never once stops halfway.

items.mnemonic_text: An old man's (耂) bent posture, deep in thought.
items.meaning_mnemonic: To <kanji>think</kanji> is to follow one <radical>old</radical> thought down a track so full of <radical>kink</radical>s that it catches and bends back on itself before it can go anywhere.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi the konbini king hates any pause in restocking, so a riddle that forces him to stop and <kanji>think</kanji> has him drumming the beeping till and moaning <reading>coo</reading>, 「<reading>こう</reading>」, until it clears.
items.description: This is 'think' in the sense of reasoning something out, considering, or weighing options, not 'think' meaning a hunch or a casual opinion.

items.mnemonic_text: Words (言) matched all around (周): to check, investigate.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You have not begun to <kanji>investigate</kanji> until your <radical>speech</radical> has gone the whole <radical>circumference</radical> of the crowd and put the same question to every face on the rim.
items.reading_mnemonic: Detective <reading>Cho</reading> only calls a case truly <kanji>investigate</kanji>d once he has looped the entire block yelling 「<reading>ちょう</reading>」 at every door, since anything less leaves a gap in the circle.
items.description: The common verb here means 'look something up' or 'check' — a word, a timetable, a fact — as often as it means a formal investigation.

items.mnemonic_text: Feathers (羽) over white (白): a bird practicing to fly, to learn.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>learn</kanji> a skill the way down becomes flight, by beating each <radical>white</radical> tuft over and over until it stiffens into a real <radical>feather</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The cobbler <reading>Shoe</reading> swears you only <kanji>learn</kanji> to resole a boot after stitching the same seam so many times you mutter 「<reading>しゅう</reading>」 in your sleep.

items.mnemonic_text: Learning (⺍) opening one's view (見): to remember, realize.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>remember</kanji> a <radical>small</radical> fact by tucking it under a <radical>cover</radical> where your roving eye can still <radical>see</radical> the lump it makes.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the shrine, Grandma Kane keeps the one phone number she still needs tucked under a sleeping cat's blanket. Each time she lifts the cover, checks it, and finds she still knows it, she gives a dry <reading>かく</reading>. That is the small <reading>cackle</reading> of someone glad her mind still works.
items.description: The active side of remember, closer to memorize or learn by heart than to passive recall.

items.mnemonic_text: A dying (亡) heart (心) losing its memory: to forget.
items.meaning_mnemonic: When a name you loved slips under the lid and joins the <radical>deceased</radical>, your <radical>heart</radical> keeps beating but you <kanji>forget</kanji> it was ever there.
items.reading_mnemonic: An old classmate waves at you on the mossy shrine steps, and you have completely forgotten his name. You stall with a slow, deep <reading>bow</reading>, your back creaking <reading>ぼう</reading> as it sinks. He bows back just as lost, and the shrine cats watch two grown adults <reading>ぼう</reading>-ing in silence, neither one admitting he forgot.

items.mnemonic_text: A wagon (軍) moving down a road (辶): to carry, one's fortune.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>carry</kanji> a stalled truck's whole load by ordering an entire <radical>army</radical> to shoulder it and <radical>advance</radical> down the road on foot.
items.reading_mnemonic: The porter is so <reading>unlucky</reading> that every crate he agrees to <kanji>carry</kanji> with a weary 「<reading>うん</reading>」 turns out to be the one packed with bricks.

items.mnemonic_text: A road (辶) release (关) sending something off: to send.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>send</kanji> a parcel by shoving it through the <radical>frontier gate</radical> and onto the winding <radical>road</radical> that runs off into country you may not enter.
items.reading_mnemonic: The tailor <reading>Sew</reading> refuses to <kanji>send</kanji> any parcel until she has stitched it shut, humming 「<reading>そう</reading>」 as the needle clears the last corner.

items.mnemonic_text: Two axes (斤斤) weighing shells (貝) of value: quality, substance.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You prove the <kanji>quality</kanji> of a hoard of old <radical>money</radical> by swinging an <radical>axe</radical> at one coin, since only solid metal dents while the fake stuff shatters.
items.reading_mnemonic: The hotel inspector <reading>Sheets</reading> rubs every pillowcase between two fingers, mutters 「<reading>しつ</reading>」, and throws out any guest whose linen is not top <kanji>quality</kanji>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At closing time, Koichi, one <radical>person</radical> behind the till, stops itemizing the shelf. Each rice ball is a little <radical>jewel</radical>, and he refuses to <radical>split</radical> them into portions. He sweeps every one into a basket: the till beeps once for the <kanji>whole</kanji> lot.
items.reading_mnemonic: The new cashier, <reading>Zen</reading>, doesn't do partial sales. He scans the whole basket in one motion, muttering 「<reading>ぜん</reading>」 under his breath every night — like a chant for clearing the entire shelf in one go.

items.mnemonic_text: Bamboo (竹) matching (合) the right response: an answer.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A written <kanji>answer</kanji> is a strip of <radical>bamboo</radical> that has to <radical>fit</radical> the question slot exactly, or the grader throws it out.
items.reading_mnemonic: Quiz host <reading>Toe</reading> is so impatient he cuts each contestant off with a sharp 「<reading>とう</reading>」 the second they land the right <kanji>answer</kanji>, before they can even finish the sentence.

items.mnemonic_text: A flag (方 side) rallying an arrow's (矢) clan together: family.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>clan</kanji> is everyone who aims an <radical>arrow</radical> in whatever <radical>direction</radical> the <radical>chevron</radical> at the top of the war banner is tilted.
items.reading_mnemonic: Uncle <reading>Zock</reading> has made himself head of the whole clan and lines every cousin up behind his banner on the mountain trail. A gust off the peak sends a shudder down the family, <reading>ぞく</reading>, <reading>ぞく</reading>, one relative after the next. He won't break formation, so the shivering just loops back to the front.
items.description: This character almost never stands alone. It works as a suffix on the end of a compound, marking a group bound by blood or by kind: a household, a tribe, an ethnic people, a band of nobles. Read it as 'the ... folk' rather than a word you say by itself.

items.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Negative</kanji> is what one hard <radical>slash</radical> makes of the <radical>stick</radical> standing in the <radical>ground</radical> once even its last <radical>drop</radical> is wiped away.
items.reading_mnemonic: A theatre critic named <reading>Foo</reading> dismisses every play with one bored puff of breath, 「<reading>ふ</reading>」, the sound everyone now uses for a <kanji>negative</kanji> verdict.
items.description: Almost always a prefix: 不 flips the following word to its opposite, like English un- or non-, and rarely stands alone.

items.mnemonic_text: Rice (米) measured with a dipper (斗): materials, a fee.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>fee</kanji> the mill charges is however many level <radical>dipper</radical>s of <radical>rice</radical> it takes to fill your sack.
items.reading_mnemonic: The miller <reading>Leo</reading> barks 「<reading>りょう</reading>」 once for every scoop he tips in. However high he counts out loud is your <kanji>fee</kanji>, so regulars turn up with insultingly small sacks.

items.mnemonic_text: A jewel (王) cut along its natural grain (里): reason, logic.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Every <radical>village</radical> settles its arguments with one <radical>king's jewel</radical> on a stump, turning it until its cracks line up into the only <kanji>logic</kanji> nobody dares dispute.
items.reading_mnemonic: Village judge <reading>Lee</reading> never explains a ruling, just grunts 「<reading>り</reading>」 and taps the jewel, as if the <kanji>logic</kanji> were far too obvious to say aloud.

items.mnemonic_text: A heart (心) pierced by a single resolved stroke: certainly necessary.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At the river crossing, a <radical>slash</radical> swinging toward your <radical>heart</radical> makes stepping aside less a choice than a <kanji>necessary</kanji> reflex.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>ひつ</reading> is the only word the riverbank ferryman ever says. He will not row you across until you beat him in a quick bout, and the moment his pole taps your chest he spits it out, clipped and flat, sounding just like <reading>hit you</reading>.
items.description: The look-alike is 心, heart or mind. 心 is the bare heart shape, a wide low curve with three loose dots and nothing crossing it. 必 adds one straight slash cutting from the upper right down through the middle, and that diagonal is the whole difference.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Aim a pig's <radical>snout</radical> at one <radical>small</radical> coin in the dirt and it roots over and <kanji>hit</kanji>s the coin dead center every time.
items.reading_mnemonic: Delivery runner <reading>Toe</reading> shouts 「<reading>とう</reading>」 every time a doorframe <kanji>hit</kanji>s him in the face, and at his sprint that is roughly once a second.

items.mnemonic_text: A woman (女) under a covering (覀): the essential point, needed.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Clamp a <radical>flat lid</radical> down over a whirling <radical>woman</radical> until only one arm fits through the gap, so the single thing she still grabs is what she truly <kanji>need</kanji>s.
items.reading_mnemonic: The dance coach <reading>Yo</reading> barks 「<reading>よう</reading>」 and slashes every step the routine does not truly <kanji>need</kanji>, leaving only the handful that survive her.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Walk <radical>one</radical> straight line and <radical>stop</radical> exactly on the mark to be counted <kanji>correct</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back in the classroom, the teacher asks who stopped exactly on the line. Sei's hand shoots up before she finishes asking, and he answers with his own name like it settles it: <reading>Sei</reading>, <reading>せい</reading> — crisp, correct, a little too pleased with himself.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Line a <radical>cross</radical>hair up on your <radical>eye</radical> and nothing in the room stays <radical>hidden</radical>, so you spot the exit <kanji>straightaway</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Mechanic <reading>Chock</reading> yanks the wheel block, barks 「<reading>ちょく</reading>」, and the van rolls <kanji>straightaway</kanji> down the drive, dead straight and gone in a second.
items.description: Straightaway covers two senses here: a straight, unbent line, and something done at once with no detour. It also colours words for being frank.

items.mnemonic_text: Thread (糸) running straight through the loom (圣): to pass through time.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The single <radical>thread</radical> strung through a monk's <radical>holy</radical> prayer beads has to <kanji>pass through</kanji> all one hundred and eight of them without ever snapping.
items.reading_mnemonic: A pilgrim named <reading>Kay</reading> grumbles 「<reading>けい</reading>」 under her breath at each of the two hundred shrine gates she still has to <kanji>pass through</kanji> before dark.

items.mnemonic_text: Thread (糸) sold (売) onward without a break: to continue.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The only way this stall knows how to <radical>sell</radical> is to keep the <radical>thread</radical> unrolling off the spool, so the sale just has to <kanji>continue</kanji> until the spool runs out.
items.reading_mnemonic: A busker called <reading>Zock</reading> shouts 「<reading>ぞく</reading>」 every time someone tries to walk off, because his one rule is that the song must <kanji>continue</kanji> until the hat is full.

items.mnemonic_text: Two people standing side by side: to compare.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You get this one for free, because the <radical>compare</radical> radical and the <kanji>compare</kanji> kanji are the very same character, so it pays to know your radicals well.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank a heron named Hina lays two fish side by side to compare their weight. A jogger asks who landed the bigger one, so Hina jabs her beak toward the old fisherman, meaning <reading>he</reading> did, and croaks a flat <reading>ひ</reading> to settle it.

items.mnemonic_text: Feet advancing (辶) among matched (巽) options: to choose.
items.meaning_mnemonic: When the trail forks and you may <radical>advance</radical> down only one branch, taking the <radical>southeast</radical> fork instead of all the others is exactly what it means to <kanji>choose</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A talent-show judge named <reading>Sen</reading> screams 「<reading>せん</reading>」 the moment she has to <kanji>choose</kanji> a winner, because cutting twelve acts down to one physically hurts her.

items.mnemonic_text: Bones (歹) left over after the cut (戔): what remains.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Dig a grave too <radical>shallow</radical> after a stroke of <radical>bad luck</radical> and part of what you buried will always <kanji>remain</kanji> poking up out of the dirt.

items.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Eight</radical> <radical>sheep</radical> stand chewing by the <radical>water</radical>. The water rises and spreads until the fence and the sheep are gone under it. It keeps going, flat and endless, until it is one giant <kanji>ocean</kanji>.

Each giggle ends the same way — a bright little <reading>き</reading>, sharp as a turning <reading>key</reading> — because that's the sound old wood makes when it remembers.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>possess</kanji> a thing only while your <radical>left hand</radical> stays clamped on it, which is why even the <radical>moon</radical> becomes yours the second you get a grip.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Hugh</reading> refuses to admit he <kanji>possess</kanji>es anything, so he keeps yelling 「<reading>ゆう</reading>」, which sounds just like 'you,' and swears every coat, cat, and cup in the house is really yours.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A foreman grips a loaded <radical>brush</radical>, ink dripping from its tip. He drags his back leg into a <radical>long stride or stretching</radical> that no real step should reach. The trailing brush inks one straight line, marking where to <kanji>build</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Ken, the sword-collecting shiba, patrols the fresh foundation line like it is one more sword for his wall. Every lap he barks <reading>けん</reading>, and the crew swears the dog is shouting his own name, <reading>Ken</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>rouse</kanji> <radical>oneself</radical> at dawn only by making your legs <radical>run</radical> for the door before the rest of you gets a vote.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kiki the tree spirit shrieks 「<reading>き</reading>！」 at first light, and the whole forest has to <kanji>rouse</kanji> itself because a giggling <reading>Kiki</reading> will not let one branch stay asleep.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Even after one <radical>slash</radical> leaves the <radical>samurai</radical> a <radical>body</radical> flat on the tatami, what carries across the hall is the <kanji>voice</kanji> that still shouts orders.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei the star student treats every 「<reading>せい</reading>」 as a cue to 「<reading>say</reading>」 something first, so hers is the only <kanji>voice</kanji> the back row ever hears.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Workers stack bars of <radical>gold</radical> in the vault. The inspector's boot hits an immovable <radical>stopping</radical> point at one duller bar. She sets that reject aside and calls it <kanji>silver</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The vault inspector introduces herself as <reading>Gin</reading>. She says it the same flat way every time she rejects a bar, <reading>ぎん</reading>, like she's already bored of the job. She's the one who decided, years ago, that silver deserved its own shelf.

items.meaning_mnemonic: When the <radical>sun</radical> sits at the exact <radical>center</radical> of the sky, the water below throws back its clearest <kanji>reflect</kanji>ion.
items.reading_mnemonic: Startled by his own doubled face in the water, the fisherman yelps 「<reading>Ay</reading>」 — 「<reading>えい</reading>」. The river throws the sound straight back at him a beat later, flat and unbothered, same as it did with the light.

items.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>England</kanji> is the one country where a flawless patch of <radical>grass</radical> mown at the dead <radical>center</radical> of the garden counts as a national achievement.
items.reading_mnemonic: A tour guide called <reading>Amy</reading> ends every fact about <kanji>England</kanji> with a proud 「<reading>えい</reading>！」, certain the country's whole name is just that one long sound stretched over a map.
items.description: Beyond the country name, this kanji means outstanding or brilliant, as in words for a hero or a gifted person. England just borrows its sound.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A farmer stacks his <radical>beans</radical> on top of a giant <radical>page</radical> torn from his ledger. The stack wobbles and splits into <radical>eight</radical> tumbling piles. One heavy pile crashes down and thumps him square on the <kanji>head</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back at the desk, a deskmate spots the bump swelling where the log struck. He winces and mutters <reading>とう</reading>, the same hiss you'd make after stubbing your <reading>toe</reading> on a desk leg.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> strides forward, then drops into a sudden crouch. They press their <radical>family name</radical> seal onto the <radical>ground</radical> instead of a desk. Bowing that low is what <kanji>lower</kanji> means.
items.reading_mnemonic: Tay, a tortoise whose shell is too heavy to lift, groans <reading>てい</reading> every time he tries to stand. It comes out flat and defeated, like the English word <reading>tay</reading>. He gives up and presses his belly back onto the ground beside the still-bowing person. Down there, low is where he stays.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A mound of <radical>earth</radical> sits on top, underneath a sealed <radical>cocoon</radical> tucked out of sight. Whatever was inside wrapped up and went under the soil. Dig the mound over: nothing is left. It is <kanji>gone</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kyo is the magician who buries things and cannot get them back. He taps the mound, says 「<reading>きょ</reading>」 with a flourish, and that is genuinely the end of the trick. No reappearance, no second half. きょ, and it is gone.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>copy</kanji> is the page you <radical>bestow</radical> on whoever asks while the real one stays hidden under its <radical>cover</radical> the whole time.
items.reading_mnemonic: A wedding photographer called <reading>Shaw</reading> shouts 「<reading>しゃ</reading>！」 as the shutter fires, so every guest he aims at becomes one more <kanji>copy</kanji> pasted in the album.
items.description: This kanji leans toward capturing an image, like a photograph, more than photocopying. It also covers copying text out by hand or describing a scene.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>child</radical> hides under the <radical>roof</radical> during a storm. Bored, she scratches a squiggly mark into the wooden wall. Her father names the strange mark their family's first <kanji>character</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma claps her hands at the wall and gasps a delighted <reading>じ</reading> — it comes out just like blurting <reading>gee</reading> at the sight — proud that the scrawled little mark is already a character worth keeping.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Once the last <radical>person</radical> outdoors presses a <radical>lid</radical> down over the fading <radical>evening</radical>, not one <radical>drop</radical> of light escapes, and the sealed black that follows is <kanji>night</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The guard on the late shift, <reading>Yah</reading>, is down to a single flat 「<reading>や</reading>」 by the time <kanji>night</kanji> falls, because twelve hours on his feet in the dark have scraped every other word out of him.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>ray</kanji> is a <radical>small</radical> bright speck set on a <radical>flat top</radical> so level that it can throw one line dead straight for miles without ever dipping.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Koichi</reading> runs his konbini lights so hard that one <kanji>ray</kanji> bouncing off the onigiri shelf can leave a spot in your vision. Told this, he says 「<reading>こう</reading>」 and reaches for the dimmer to turn it up.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> steps onto the thawed <radical>ground</radical> after a long winter. They plant <radical>two</radical> sticks and throw their arms out as <radical>big</radical> as they can. The <radical>sun</radical> climbs higher each morning until mud season turns into <kanji>springtime</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A groundhog named <reading>Shun</reading> pokes up from his burrow the moment the yard warms, shouts <reading>しゅん</reading>, and dives straight back down out of pure habit. He shuns the cold on principle, but there isn't any today — the mud outside smells exactly like the springtime the person just stepped into.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A stalk of <radical>grain</radical> leans over and drops onto the <radical>fire</radical> burning beside the field. It catches fast and sends smoke drifting over the empty rows. That smoky smell means <kanji>autumn</kanji> has arrived.
items.reading_mnemonic: A scarecrow standing in the smoking field flaps its sleeves at circling crows and yells <reading>shoo</reading>, <reading>しゅう</reading>, over and over until they scatter. Smoke from the burning stalks stings its painted eyes, but it keeps shouting anyway — the last of the grain only survives if somebody protects it.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Your bare feet scorch on the baked <radical>ground</radical>. You point at <radical>self</radical> and swear the heat does not bother you. Then your <radical>trailing foot</radical> drags behind, and the stubborn heat becomes <kanji>summer</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, sags on a power line above that same baked ground. Too hot even for him, he cracks his beak and a weak puff of flame escapes with a scorched <reading>か</reading>. That tired flame-cough is how you remember summer's reading, <reading>か</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Because a <radical>lad</radical> this vain only ever grooms the side of his <radical>head</radical> that people see, every hair on his <kanji>face</kanji> is perfect and the back is a mess.
items.reading_mnemonic: On class-photo day at the school the photographer levels his camera like a <reading>gun</reading> and shouts 「<reading>がん</reading>」 until every kid aims a <kanji>face</kanji> straight down the lens.

items.meaning_mnemonic: An <radical>arrow</radical> hits a target and snaps in half, the pieces splitting apart like <radical>eight</radical>. The stub falls into a bowl of <radical>beans</radical> and looks tiny beside a whole one. Cut off before its time, the little arrow stays <kanji>short</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The vendor is a wiry guy everyone calls <reading>Tan</reading>. Every time he pulls another snapped stub from the bowl, he mutters <reading>たん</reading> under his breath. He's annoyed at how short his profits look today.
items.description: Beyond literal shortness, 短 also carries the sense of a shortcoming. It's the kind of short that comes up when someone lists a personality flaw or weak point, not just a measurement of length.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> who can <radical>renew</radical> anything for you without leaving the counter is selling pure <kanji>convenience</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The badger's slam sends the vending machine's change chute rattling out coins. The hiker who planned to buy one — a guy named <reading>Ben</reading> — just mutters 「<reading>べん</reading>」 under his breath, resigned to waiting outside in the rain.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>evening</radical> radical you already learned and the <kanji>evening</kanji> kanji are the same character, so knowing your radicals cold just handed you this one for free.
items.reading_mnemonic: The shrine sweeper <reading>Seki</reading> clocks in at exactly 「<reading>せき</reading>」 past sunset, never a minute early, so her entire shift is one long <kanji>evening</kanji> of shooing cats off the mossy steps.

items.meaning_mnemonic: This is the <radical>meat</radical> radical and the <kanji>meat</kanji> kanji at once, one shape doing both jobs, so you already know it from the butcher's-shop window.
items.reading_mnemonic: Regulars at the butcher counter groan his name, 「<reading>にく</reading>」, every time <reading>Nick, ooh</reading> leans a thumb on the scale and the <kanji>meat</kanji> jumps a whole kilo.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The plaza of <radical>earth</radical> is held in high <radical>esteem</radical> by the whole town. A crowd fills it, too big for the open sky above. Someone stretches a giant <radical>cover</radical> across it, and it becomes the <kanji>public chamber</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Under the same blanket-roofed hall, a baker elbows in holding a fresh lump of <reading>dough</reading>, insisting the shrine crowd taste it. Everyone groans one long <reading>どう</reading>, half hunger, half surrender, and makes room for him anyway.
items.description: This kanji almost never stands alone. In real use it is nearly always the second half of a compound naming one specific large room — a dining hall, a lecture hall — rather than a generic public chamber on its own.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>bird</radical> radical and the <kanji>bird</kanji> kanji are the same character, and it also means chicken, because a chicken is just the bird you are most likely to eat.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the shrine a fat cat named <reading>Chow</reading> watches the pigeons land and rumbles 「<reading>ちょう</reading>」, since as far as she is concerned a <kanji>bird</kanji> is just lunch that has not noticed her yet.

items.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Winter</kanji> is the one season your <radical>trailing foot</radical> drags a strip of <radical>ice</radical> across the floor with every step you take indoors.
items.reading_mnemonic: A hiker called <reading>Toe</reading> reaches the mountain-trail vending machine with both of hers gone numb and barks 「<reading>とう</reading>」, because nothing but deep <kanji>winter</kanji> freezes feet through two pairs of socks.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>dog</kanji> is a <radical>big</radical> animal so shapeless that the single wet <radical>drop</radical> of its nose is the only way to find its front end.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Ken</reading> the shiba inu only guards his wall of antique swords for someone who can bark 「<reading>けん</reading>」 exactly right, because no <kanji>dog</kanji> this fussy about blades will answer a sloppy call.

items.meaning_mnemonic: It turns <kanji>sultry</kanji> when <radical>someone</radical> is pinned in an open field and the <radical>sun</radical> bakes the damp air around them for hours.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Show</reading> the weatherman does his forecast live from a treeless field, so overheated that the one syllable he can force out, 「<reading>しょ</reading>」, is now the station's official word for a <kanji>sultry</kanji> afternoon.
items.description: This is heat from the air or the weather, not from a hot object. Something hot to the touch, like a pan or a kettle, is written with another kanji entirely.

items.meaning_mnemonic: It is so <kanji>cold</kanji> under the <radical>roof</radical> that the <radical>well</radical> freezes to <radical>ice</radical>, and the swelling ice <radical>splits</radical> the <radical>ground</radical> beneath the house.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the mountain-trail vending machine, a drink frozen too solid to pour rings out 「<reading>かん</reading>」 when you knock it, and that hollow <reading>can</reading>-knock is the sound of the whole trail going <kanji>cold</kanji>.
items.description: This is the cold you feel all over, from cold weather or an unheated room. A single cold thing you touch, like a drink or a metal rail, is a different kanji.

items.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Sino-</kanji> names the land where a <radical>husband</radical> farms the <radical>grass</radical> by the <radical>water</radical> and every <radical>mouth</radical> for miles drinks from that one river.
items.reading_mnemonic: A loud warlord called <reading>Khan</reading> stamps 「<reading>かん</reading>」 on every scroll, teapot, and character that ever came out of China, so his one syllable is now the mark of anything <kanji>Sino-</kanji>.
items.description: Sino- is the combining form of 'Chinese', and this kanji points to Han China in particular. In a few set compounds it instead means 'a man', often a rough one.
